comments.author: Jaden
comments.text:
Hey Product Hunt! 👋

We’re the PixVerse team. Meet **PixVerse R2**: a real-time world model you can explore and change while it’s being generated.

**Explore. Change. Keep going.**

*   **Explore with WASD.** Move through the world and choose where to go next.
    
*   **Change it with a prompt.** Introduce a new element or change the scene as it unfolds.
    
*   **Keep going.** Continue interacting in the same evolving world after each change.
    

A collection of R2-powered worlds is now open to explore. [**Try R2 →**](https://world.pixverse.video/)

**How R2 works**

R2 builds its world-model capabilities through continuous pretraining with Omni Causal AR, then distills that same foundation for real-time interaction. The aim is to make worlds more persistent, controllable, and scalable.

[Read the technical report →](https://pixverse.ai/en/blog/pixverse-r2-scaling-real-time-omni-world-models)

Whether you’re experimenting with interactive stories, game prototypes, or AI worlds, we’d love your feedback. **What would you explore or change first?**

_The gallery combines AI concept scenes with an overview of R2’s architecture._

comments.text: Quiver runs on Next.js, the Vercel AI SDK, Vercel Cron, Preview Deployments, and the Domains API. It is multi-tenant, with a dedicated subdomain for every workspace, so routing was the hard infrastructure problem. Host-based middleware resolves the workspace; AI responses stream from the default runtime; Cron runs scheduled work; and when a workspace is created, Quiver attaches its subdomain through the Domains API so certificate provisioning happens automatically. Without Vercel, I would have needed to operate a proxy for tenant subdomains, certificate automation, a scheduler, and separate streaming infrastructure—none of which is the product. Vercel let me focus on building Quiver's developer marketing system. Preview Deployments also shaped the product: every change gets a review URL before production, mirroring Quiver's own Draft → Review → Live workflow.

comments.text:
[@curiouskitty](https://www.producthunt.com/@curiouskitty) these are really great questions! Thank you for asking so thoughtfully because it allows me to speak on some of my favorite features of Quiver. 

The important distinction is that Quiver **proposes learning; it doesn’t silently learn**.

**From research:** when you add a call, survey, review, or support thread, Quiver analyzes it against the active context. It extracts themes, verbatim customer language, product signals, and evidence that validates or challenges active hypotheses. If that evidence suggests a context change, it creates a proposal with the **current value, proposed value, rationale, and source**.

**From performance:** when you log campaign or content results—metrics, qualitative notes, what worked, and what didn’t—Quiver runs the same kind of synthesis. Again, the result is a pending proposal, not an automatic rewrite.

On the Context page, you review each proposal side by side: **Current vs. Proposed**, with the reason behind it. You can approve or reject it. Approval creates a new context version; rejection changes nothing. Version history records the source, change summary, and timestamp. You can inspect any previous snapshot and restore it—restoration creates another version rather than deleting history.

That approval boundary is how we avoid overlearning from one-off results. One anomalous post or customer comment may raise a proposal, but it cannot become organizational truth on its own. You can reject it, leave the existing hypothesis in place, or wait for repeated evidence. Quiver isn’t secretly fine-tuning a model on your activity—the “learning” is explicit, evidence-linked, versioned, and reversible.
